A recommendation is a statement in which someone tells another person that something — a product, a person, a place, a course of action — is good, suitable, or worth choosing.

When you make a recommendation, you are essentially saying: "I think this is a good choice for you. You should consider it."

A recommendation has three key elements:

  1. A recommender — the person or body giving the suggestion.
  2. A recipient — the person who receives the suggestion and may act on it.
  3. The thing being endorsed — what is being suggested as good or appropriate.

Crucially, a recommendation is not a command or an order. The person receiving it is free to accept or reject it. It is a guided suggestion, not a requirement.

Understanding what a recommendation is not helps you understand it more sharply.

  • Opinion vs. Recommendation: An opinion is simply what you think or feel ("I think this movie is great"). A recommendation goes one step further — it is an opinion that also urges someone to take an action ("I think you should watch this movie"). All recommendations contain an opinion, but not all opinions are recommendations.
  • Advice vs. Recommendation: Advice is general guidance about what to do in a situation ("You should eat healthier"). A recommendation is more specific and often more formal — it points to a particular choice ("I recommend this brand of oats"). In practice, the two words overlap a lot, but a recommendation tends to be more direct and definitive.
  • Request vs. Recommendation: A request asks you to do something for the speaker. A recommendation suggests what you should do for your own benefit.
  • Instruction vs. Recommendation: An instruction tells you exactly what to do and often implies you must follow it. A recommendation is advisory — it guides but does not compel.

A recommendation carries the credibility and trust of the person giving it. When a doctor recommends a medicine, a teacher recommends a book, or a trusted friend recommends a restaurant, the advice carries weight because the recommender has relevant knowledge, experience, or authority.

This is why a recommendation from an expert or a trusted person feels more valuable than a random suggestion. The stronger the recommender's credibility, the more seriously the recommendation is taken.

Recommendations appear in many areas of life:

1. Informal, everyday recommendations
These happen in conversation between friends, family, or colleagues.

  • "You should try that new café on the corner — the coffee is excellent."
  • "I highly recommend this book. It changed how I think about habits."

2. Professional recommendations
These come from experts in a field — doctors, lawyers, financial advisors, consultants — who use their knowledge to guide a client's decision.

  • A doctor might say: "My recommendation is to rest for two weeks and avoid strenuous activity."
  • A financial advisor might recommend a particular investment strategy.

3. Formal written recommendations (Letters of Recommendation)
This is a very specific and common use of the word. A letter of recommendation (also called a reference letter) is a formal document in which someone — usually a teacher, employer, or mentor — writes about another person's qualities, abilities, and character, and endorses them for a job, a university, a scholarship, or an award.

In this context, "recommendation" means: I am officially vouching for this person's suitability.

4. Official / institutional recommendations
Governments, health organizations, and scientific bodies issue official recommendations based on research and expertise.

  • The World Health Organization issues health recommendations.
  • A government might issue dietary recommendations for its citizens.
  • A court might make a sentencing recommendation.

These carry authority and are taken very seriously, though individuals and institutions are still free to follow or ignore them.

5. Algorithmic / technology recommendations
In the modern world, recommendation also refers to the suggestions made by software systems.

  • When YouTube suggests a video, or Amazon suggests a product, or Spotify suggests a song, these are called recommendations.
  • The system behind this is called a recommendation engine or recommendation algorithm.

"Recommendation" can appear as singular or plural.

  • Recommendation — one specific suggestion.

"The doctor gave me a recommendation to see a specialist."

  • Recommendations — a set of suggestions, often at the end of a report or study.

"The committee's recommendations were submitted to the board."

In formal reports, business documents, or research papers, a dedicated section titled "Recommendations" is common. It contains the writer's proposed actions based on the findings of the report.

• To make a recommendation — to suggest something.

"Can you make a recommendation for a good hotel in Delhi?"

  • To follow a recommendation — to do what was suggested.

"She followed her doctor's recommendation and started exercising daily."

  • To act on a recommendation — to take action based on the suggestion.

"The company acted on the consultant's recommendations immediately."

  • On the recommendation of someone — because someone suggested it.

"He was hired on the recommendation of the senior manager."

  • A strong recommendation — a very firm or enthusiastic endorsement.

"She gave him a strong recommendation for the position."

  • A recommendation letter / letter of recommendation — a formal written endorsement of a person.
  • At someone's recommendation — the same as "on the recommendation of."

"At her teacher's recommendation, she applied to the advanced program."

A recommendation is a suggestion or endorsement that tells someone a particular choice, action, person, or thing is good, suitable, or worth pursuing. It comes from someone with knowledge, experience, or authority. It is advisory — not binding — meaning the recipient can choose whether to follow it. It appears in everyday conversation, professional contexts, formal letters, official reports, and digital technology.

The heart of the word is this: someone who knows better, or has experienced something, is pointing you toward what they believe is the right or best choice.
